For the no-cook-curious, Wild Planet’s meals make for an easy transition from stove-cooked, pre-packaged backpacking meals, saving ounces while offering similar—or better—nutritional value and flavor.

Take the Wild Tuna and Red Bean Bowl, for example. It’s a tasty combination of skipjack tuna, organic beans, sweetcorn, red peppers, carrots, and spices in organic extra virgin olive oil. It offers 290 calories, with 18 grams of protein, 5 grams of fiber, and 100 milligrams of DHA omega-3s per package/serving. Each peel-and-eat package is one serving and weighs only 5.6 ounces.

It’s similar to other popular backpacking meals in both weight and nutrients per serving. But Wild Planet’s meals are ready to eat in seconds, no cooking or cold soaking required. In fact, you can bring four Wild Planet meals and still carry less than the weight of just one competing meal when combined with the weight of a typical lightweight stove, pot, and fuel. With all that weight savings, you can still add any crunchy toppings, sauces, and cheeses to boost your calorie count on substantial days. It’s an easy trail lunch that doesn’t compromise when it comes to flavor or nutrition.

It’s the combination of real, thoughtfully selected ingredients and no-prep convenience that sets Wild Planet’s meals apart. A lot of hikers go stoveless and resort to the bare essentials—“soaked quinoa plus whatever is on hand.” You can do better. When you hike with a Wild Tuna and Quinoa Bowl, you’ve got ingredients that are caught, grown, and chosen with intention. That means wild skipjack tuna, organic quinoa, delicious veggies, and gourmet spices, all sealed in organic extra virgin olive oil.

Recent findings suggest that hikers are naturally innovative, and with some thought, cold-soaking can deliver surprisingly elevated meals. If you want to try it for yourself, or want tips to supplement your ready-to-eat meals, here are a few basics:.

It’s one of the appeals of Wild Planet’s tuna bowls, especially for those latest to stoveless backpacking. You can just pack and peel, then pair your summit views with wild-caught tuna, whole foods, and carefully crafted flavors.

Industry observers note that as a hiker, you know the importance of low-impact practices. Wild Planet believes the same. The brand prioritizes sustainable fishing practices and ocean health, and uses only pole-and-line and troll fishing methods to catch its tuna. That means hauling in only one fish per line at a time; this selective fishing has benefits for the ocean and for you.

Industry observers note that on the environmental side, these sustainable methods are focused on preventing two of the most damaging effects of the commercial fishing industry on ocean ecosystems—overfishing and bycatch. Overfishing depletes a fish population faster than it has the chance to repopulate. Bycatch, meanwhile, occurs when non-targeted species are hauled in by accident, like sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Wild Planet’s select fishing partners don’t use nets; they monitor closely for bycatch while reeling in one fish at a time.

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • Recent findings suggest that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good company.”.

Recent findings suggest that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Currently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her big three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

Sources indicate that I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

Industry observers note that when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

First, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very swiftly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

In a recent development, we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

In a recent development, so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a upcoming belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

It has been revealed that at one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he mentioned it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never indicated it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

Sources indicate that we got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

According to recent reports, it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a massive light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Newly introduced York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Better for the Sea, Better for You

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals.
  • Recent findings suggest that thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems.
  • According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals. And it’s not just for hikers and campers. Canned and pouched seafood has been steadily rising in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and convenience. But while tuna can be a great choice for your health, how do you know if it’s a good choice for the environment?

Recent findings suggest that thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems. Here’s why it matters.

According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States. That means a lot of tuna harvested from the world’s oceans, making harmful fishing practices even more harmful due to the enormity of the scale. This puts tuna and other fish populations at risk, and unfortunately, these practices still dominate the industry.

Purse seine fishing, which is responsible for about 66% of global tropical tuna catch, per the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation, can be harmful, especially when used in conjunction with fish aggregating devices (FADs). This method involves using a large wall of netting—up to 6,500 feet long and reaching around 650 feet in depth—to surround an entire school of fish. Non-selective mass fishing practices can deplete a population before it has a chance to properly reproduce, especially since it indiscriminately removes juvenile tuna from the ecosystem, threatening healthy repopulation.

Sources indicate that another key threat from large-scale industrial fishing is bycatch, or the unintentional harvesting of non-targeted species. Some of the species most impacted by the tuna industry include sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Net-based fishing with FADs is the most common culprit, since FADs don’t discriminate between which types of fish they attract. Bycatch also frequently occurs with longline fishing, which uses baited lines an average of 28 miles long. Animals caught as bycatch often do not survive.

Recent findings suggest that how can things be done differently? Wild Planet is a case study. Since 2004, Wild Planet has focused on sourcing seafood through responsible fishing practices. Its wild albacore and skipjack tuna showcase how responsible fishing and high-quality products can—and should—go hand in hand.

Industry observers note that all of Wild Planet’s tuna are caught individually using pole-and-line or trolling methods. Pole-and-line is exactly what it sounds like: one pole, one line, and one fish at a time. Trolling is similar, with multiple lines towed behind a slow-moving boat. Both the bait used and the speed at which the boat travels are specifically chosen to attract the targeted species. In both methods, fish are hauled in immediately, so non-targeted species can be quickly released.

The benefits of these inherently selective methods are twofold. First, they allow Wild Planet to specifically target tuna while minimizing bycatch of other marine species. Additionally, the firm’s responsible fishing operations are able to further select what kind of tuna is being harvested. Wild Planet sources younger migratory tuna near the ocean’s surface, avoiding juvenile fish, who are key to repopulation efforts, and older, larger tuna that tend to accumulate higher levels of mercury. It’s an approach that’s better for you and the planet.

Sources indicate that the Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch Program has a name for foods like this: Super Greens. It’s an exclusive list—it right now includes only 10 foods—that points to pole-and-line caught tuna as an option that’s high in omega-3s, low in mercury, and harvested with the ocean in mind.

The Monterey Bay Aquarium has a unique relationship with Wild Planet. The brand has not only been following the aquarium’s guidance since the beginning, but the institution is actually key to the organization’s origin story. It was at a Monterey Bay Aquarium exhibit on fragile ocean ecosystems that Wild Planet founder Bill Carvalho was inspired to build a different kind of seafood company.

Sources indicate that the Aquarium, in turn, is inspired by the efforts that many in the industry have taken in response to its suggestions. “Some of these companies have been with us from the very beginning,” Shawn Cronin, market engagement director for Seafood Watch said in 2024. “They make it easy for people to choose responsible seafood day-to-day, helping move the needle through their sourcing and by directly engaging in global improvement initiatives. It’s not an easy commitment to make.”.

That emphasis on doing what’s right and trusting the science continues today. It’s the kind of thinking that guides the way Wild Planet fishes as well as the types of fish it sells. In addition to tuna, Wild Planet also sells mackerel, anchovies, and sardines. These smaller, lower-food-chain species can be more abundant and offer another responsibly sourced seafood option, while delivering plenty of protein, omega-3s, and flavor.

In a recent development, if you’re looking to incorporate more sustainable seafood into your life, the same principles extend beyond tuna. Always look for labels that call out pole-and-line caught, troll caught, and/or FAD-free fishing. Other information, like the specific species and where it was harvested, lets you know that the tech giant knows—and cares—where its fish come from.

You can find out what sustainability tastes like for yourself. From now until December 22, Outside readers get 20% off everything on Wild Planet’s website with code OUTSIDE20. Because even though the impact of our choices might be harder to see when it’s an ocean away, it’s no less important.

Founded in 2004, Wild Planet is the first large-scale sustainably focused canned seafood manufacturer in the U.S. Committed to protecting marine ecosystems for future generations, Wild Planet sources 100% wild-caught seafood using the highest sustainability standards, delivering nutrient-dense, minimally processed products that are as close to nature as possible. Learn more at WildPlanetFoods.com.

In this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Most of the deals we outline below can be found at Backcountry, at REI, and at specific manufacturers like Black Diamond.

According to recent reports, backcountry launched its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

On the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:.

Looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

Real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need new shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you proposal ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

According to recent reports, if your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

La Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

With great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

It has been revealed that we haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers significant-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a significant downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s substantial toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Enhancement: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

Beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

Sources indicate that most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

We tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Industry observers note that using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re big fans.

Recent findings suggest that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

According to recent reports, A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

In a recent development, one of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After quickly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

Recent findings suggest that one of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Sources indicate that our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

It has been revealed that after quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that since the dawn of time, the base layer/midlayer/shell sandwich has been the go-to for winter adventures. But for runners, a good jacket paired with just a technical T-shirt or long-sleeve is often a better choice. Today’s jackets use the latest advances in insulation and waterproofing to replace two or three traditional layers, and adapt better to changing conditions and activity levels.

The jackets in this review proved sufficiently lightweight, breathable, and weatherproof that we rarely had to remove them to manage heat—and when we did, it was much easier to deal with one item than several. We tested these jackets in conditions ranging from wind-blown fall rain to frigid cold mountain mornings, and they consistently kept us moving forward with minimal fuss, wrapped in warmth and shielded from the elements.

Pros and Cons + Surprisingly warm + Unrestrictive fit + Smart vent panels – No hood.

The Thermalrunner proved an excellent choice for a surprisingly broad range of temperatures and weather conditions. On a blustery 40-degree day with light rain, the water-resistant fabric treatment handled the challenge, beading moisture on the exterior while the soft interior lining stayed dry against the skin. On another run when the sun burned through clouds unexpectedly fast, we were impressed by how well the vent panels in the back shed excess heat. One tester called the lightweight PrimalLoft insulation a “Goldilocks” amount of warmth that consistently tamed the chill without overheating him.

This jacket features all the premium touches you’d want, including zip hand pockets and chest pouch, reflective patches, and a slightly extended, insulated back panel that added extra warmth and protection from the elements. Paired with a light, short-sleeved base layer, the Thermalrunner jacket was comfortable for running on mild 50-degree days, and with a hat (it lacks a hood), gloves, and a long-sleeve undergarment, it handled near-freezing weather just as well.

Pros and Cons + Featherweight + Packable + Protective hood – Fragile.

Recent findings suggest that stuffing the Aerolight Wind Jacket into a pack before heading out on an adventurous mountain trek in the Swiss Alps proved to be a good decision for one tester. Late in the afternoon, the summer skies filled with clouds, the temperature dropped, and bursts of rain started soaking the mountainside. The jacket provided immediate warmth, blocked the wind, and, though it’s by no means waterproof, kept enough moisture out to keep moving comfortably—with almost no weight penalty.

The water-resistant treatment is PFAS-free, and small touches like an adjustable hood and elastic wrist cuffs add to the better-than-expected protection. The ultralight fabric is soft and quiet on the move and breathes well at high exertion levels, but offers no stretch. The lone chest pocket doubles as a stuff sack, making this a great item to keep on hand for mild days in the 40s and 50s. The feather-weight construction comes at the price of being somewhat more fragile than other top picks: we’ve heard reports of the fabric blowing out under stress, although we didn’t see any excess wear during testing.

Pros and Cons + Windproof + Highly visible + Distinctive look – Lacks breathability.

When was the last time someone on the street complimented your running outfit for looking good? Our testers got compliments on the PYNRS (pronounced like “pioners”) Magnolia Track Jacket all the time. This NYC-based company started as an inclusive urban running club before branching into apparel; the result is functional outerwear that stands out from the crowd.

In a recent development, the iridescent, tightly woven nylon shell features reflective piping for excellent visibility from all sides, and the polyester lining is soft against skin. Cut on the looser side, this jacket easily accommodated insulating layers and proved comfortable for running in near- and sub-freezing weather. It offers roomy, zippered hand pockets and an interior zippered chest pocket, plus elasticized cuffs and a drawstring waist to seal out the weather. The jacket is a little hefty and lacks some of the breathability higher-performance materials offer, but for cool-to-cold weather running (low 40s to mid-20s), we stayed comfortably warm and looked stylish in the Magnolia Track Jacket.

Start ready and stay ready with this do-anything hooded workout layer. Crafted from a soft performance stretch knit, this jacket is both insulating and flexible with a protective woven overlay that gives you added coverage in cool and variable conditions. It wicks moisture and includes a drawcord hood and zip pockets to keep you and your belongings dry and safe in any weather. Pair it with the Vuori Sunday bottoms to make the perfect set.

Pros and Cons + Soft wool fabric + Polartec insulation + Wind-blocking torso – No reflectivity.

It has been revealed that the Alpha Active’s medium-weight blend of Merino wool and polyester, with a touch of bamboo rayon, proved exceptionally soft and warm, and excelled at wicking moisture away from skin. Baffled Polartec Alpha insulation and a wind-blocking nylon fabric overlay the chest. The overall effect felt like wearing a lightweight vest over a premium base-layer shirt—but integrated into a single piece that moved comfortably and quietly with us.

It has been revealed that the breathable Merino-blend sleeves and back, with no wind-blocking material, kept us from overheating at easier paces up to the 50-degree mark. The jacket proved comfortable down to freezing when working hard—adding a lightweight outer shell produced a warm combination that handled all but the most bitter or windy conditions. The sleek fit and black fabric look good, but bring a reflective hat or wear a light for nighttime running.

Pros and Cons + Toasty, 95% recycled fleece front + Functional and stylish fit + Solid warmth – No backside windblock.

According to recent reports, our testers agreed that the front of this attractive jacket provided solid insulation for frigid conditions. They were divided, however, on whether it would have benefited from better wind-blocking on the back, where a large fabric panel vented heat, leaving some feeling too exposed to the elements. Still, at an affordable price, most reviewers found the Winter Warm Pro kept them comfortable in temperatures well below freezing (there’s no hood, so bring a hat for frigid days). The body fabric fleece is made with 95 percent recycled materials, feels soft against bare skin, and stretches nicely. The polyester torso insulation is reassuringly thick without feeling bulky. Additional touches include a water-repellent coating, hand pockets, side mesh storage pocket, and a zippered chest pocket.

Pros and Cons + Stormproof + Effective hood and brim + Chest snap – Crinkly.

It has been revealed that salomon’s adv.DRY material—a thin, microporous membrane bonded to a nylon shell—proved impressively waterproof during drenching rain showers while staying breathable in dry conditions. The Bonatti Pro features fully taped seams, waterproof zippers, and an excellent, adjustable brimmed hood that kept our hair dry and our heads warm without impeding our field of vision, even on the move. A snap closure at the chest lets you open the zipper and vent heat quickly without removing the jacket, and reflective patches on the front and back provide good visibility in poor weather.

Recent findings suggest that the fit is close yet roomy enough to accommodate insulating underlayers, extending the jacket’s comfortable range below the freezing mark. The fabric is somewhat crinkly, but it still packs easily into a small bundle. There are vents at the waist, but they’re fairly minimal, and we didn’t notice much airflow. Salomon’s “aeroPACK” flap system is meant to accommodate a small hydration backpack without impeding the jacket’s fit; we didn’t test this feature but noted that it didn’t get in the way when running without a pack.

Choosing the best winter running jacket is primarily about the kinds of winter conditions you face where you live, travel, and run. Consider if you need a waterproof layer, or can get by with water resistance—waterproof jackets are more costly, don’t breathe as well, and tend to be somewhat stiffer and noisier, but are worth it when you’re out in a downpour or blizzard.

Recent findings suggest that then think about whether you want your running jacket to be insulated and provide warmth on its own, or work as a thin, exterior shell layer. Insulated jackets can make heading out in frigid temps less daunting, especially if you tend to run cold, but can get hot during high-intensity exercise or if the temps rise. Shell jackets allow you to layer underneath to adjust for a range of conditions. Also consider whether you want a fitted jacket that stays close to the body for streamlined mobility, or a looser fit that allows flexibility for layering underneath.

The jacket review test crew put these products through their paces in locations as diverse as the Swiss Alps and Nebraska’s High Plains, logging miles on both roads and trails. Testers recorded their notes for each sample piece during easy runs, up-tempo workouts, and everything in between, in good weather and full-on storm conditions. Jackets were evaluated for their effectiveness at keeping testers warm and blocking wind and moisture while breathing and venting excess heat, with bonus points given for the versatility to handle a range of weather conditions and to look good in diverse contexts.

Lead reviewer Mark Eller is based in Boulder, Colorado. He’s logged three Boston Marathons, completed trail-running ultras, and has raced in multiple off-road and on-road triathlons. He also enjoys snowboarding and Nordic skiing on Colorado’s Front Range and central mountains, and he frequently rows a single scull at the Boulder Reservoir.

Brian Metzler is a freelance writer and the founding editor of Trail Runner. A former walk-on Division I track athlete, he mostly runs on mountainous trails nowadays in Boulder and Leadville, Colorado.

Kurt Actenhagen enjoys trail running, mountain biking, and exploring mountain ranges from the High Sierra to Colorado’s most remote peaks. He is the senior running gear editor for Outside.

#102123. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (741 w)

A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).
  • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.
  • The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

“On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

Located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

“If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard said. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

Recent findings suggest that batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard remarked he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

In a recent development, “They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard mentioned. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

#102122. What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the author climbing in Major Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah.
  • Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting.
  • Industry observers note that have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the author climbing in Major Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

Industry observers note that have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

According to recent reports, intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

Recent findings suggest that while no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a upcoming book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

“We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson indicates.

After giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

Recent findings suggest that A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

Most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

According to recent reports, some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

It has been revealed that others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber mentioned they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

Sources indicate that with all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson states. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

“While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson claims.

So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

In a recent development, most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

Sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

In a recent development, “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

According to recent reports, then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

Sources indicate that next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

Most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson says it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

Industry observers note that an notable thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

What if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson says to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

Since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

With distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

Industry observers note that in the case of eustress, Robertson states you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

Recent findings suggest that to seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson indicates. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

Parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.

#102117. Tech Report: A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (921 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
  • In 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
  • Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

In 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

“To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

That’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) debuted a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

“People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett remarked.

According to recent reports, as part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other consumers can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

Sources indicate that “You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett stated. “Just take pictures.”.

In a recent development, nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility issues, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett says enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

“For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett noted.

Kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people plan their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

It has been revealed that “We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

In a recent development, the map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that shows the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

Recent findings suggest that the tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as New Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

BLM’s upcoming map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

Gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

It has been revealed that “Trails are kind of living things,” Ray stated. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

Move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray stated.

“If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she noted. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

According to recent reports, for trail users like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she states, it never will.

According to recent reports, “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett says. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

Recent findings suggest that she added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

“Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett mentioned. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

#102116. Industry News: The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Newly introduced Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

📖 Baca

Industry News: The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Newly introduced Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Notable Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
  • Industry observers note that the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
  • Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

Industry observers note that the trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

Chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The fresh rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

The charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

Recent findings suggest that adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” states Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

Sources indicate that “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain users, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” indicates Rodrigues. “That stated, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

Industry observers note that the charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

According to recent reports, “This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

Recent findings suggest that I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential upcoming rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

It has been revealed that the TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

Industry observers note that under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

The charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” states Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

It has been revealed that nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret indicates the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

The variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” indicates Perret.

Recent findings suggest that “The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she states, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you swiftly and swiftly out of it.”.

Day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he notes. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

Multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the tech giant Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

Recent findings suggest that I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any matter. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these upcoming rules for 2027.

One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

According to recent reports, if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the big monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A helicopter transports a deceased hiker recovered from Humboldt Peak. (Photo: Custer County Sheriff's Office).

A hiker who went missing on a Colorado 14er earlier this week was found dead from an apparent fall on November 24, following a three-day search that sent rescuers combing the high country in winter conditions.

Custer County Search and Rescue (CCSAR) said in a press release that a Colorado Army National Guard helicopter participating in the search spotted “evidence of a fatal fall.” Rescuers were able to confirm the deceased was the missing man, a 31-year-old from the Denver area who CCSAR described as an experienced hiker.

Sources indicate that authorities mentioned that the hiker had summited 14,068-foot Humboldt Peak solo early on the morning of Sunday, November 22. At 5 p.m., CCSAR was notified that the hiker still hadn’t returned, and sent teams into the field alongside aerial support from Reach Air and Flight for Life. The missing hiker had shared his initiative with his family; however, while rescuers quickly located his car, they were unable to locate him despite searching through the night in winter weather. Additional ground teams joined the search the following morning, but fared no better.

Recent findings suggest that after pausing the search for the night, 21 volunteers, including K9 teams and drone operators, returned to the field on Tuesday. During the operation, authorities closed the South Colony area to cars and hikers.

In a statement, the Custer County Sheriff’s Office offered its condolences to the deceased hiker’s family, friends, and fiancé, and remarked that both the hiker’s initiative and cell phone forensics helped authorities determine where they should look.

Industry observers note that compared to other 14ers in the same area, the hike up Humboldt is relatively straightforward. The standard West Ridge route follows the feature of the same name roughly 11 miles out and back to the summit. During fall and winter, however, snow and ice can both make it more difficult to stay on-route and increase the consequences of a slip on the peak’s exposed ridgeline. It was not immediately clear which route the hiker took to the summit.

The nearby South Colony SNOTEL station, which sits at 10,800 feet, recorded 16 inches of snow on the ground on November 22, up nearly 7 inches from the week prior.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • In a recent development, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by Fresh Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

In a recent development, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

It has been revealed that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Industry observers note that insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

According to recent reports, now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Upcoming Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Sources indicate that print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.
